messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 53‑year‑old social worker from the Midwest, had spent most of his adult life helping others navigate difficult transitions. He was married, shared a modest home with his wife, and had a steady routine that began each day with a brisk walk through the neighborhood, checking the traffic lights and the bus schedule before heading to the county shelter where he spent his mornings. The first time he was a victim, he was in his late twenties, a student studying criminal justice. While walking home after a late lecture, a man he had met on campus stepped into his path. He stopped, turned to face him, and in a single motion lunged, grabbing David’s shoulder and forcing his hands against his back. The assault was swift, brutal, and the man fled into a narrow alley that closed with a rusted metal door at its end. David was left shaking, the air cold and thick with the smell of alley trash, and he heard the echo of the stranger’s footsteps fading into the night. The memory of that moment has never fully faded. Every time he recalls the grip on his shoulder, the sound of the alley door slamming, and the sudden darkness that swallowed the street, he feels an immediate surge of terror that is almost identical to the panic he felt then. Words fail him; he can only remember fragments—his hands clenched, the rough skin of the assailant, the metallic taste that lingers in his mouth. The shame that surfaces when he thinks of the violation is overwhelming, a feeling that it was his fault that something so awful could happen to him. This intrusive recollection is the starting point for a loop that has come to dominate David’s daily life. The remembrance of the assault does not merely bring back the terror; it also fuels a heightened sense of threat. As soon as he thinks of the alley, his mind races to imagine that the same man might reappear, or that someone else could replicate the violence. This perception of danger triggers his first maladaptive strategy: avoidance of enclosed spaces. He now refuses to go through the downtown subway, the cramped stairwell at the shelter, or even the small meeting rooms he once used to discuss case plans. He replaces those spaces with wide, open halls, or the bright, airy windows of the community center. When his mind drifts toward the memory, the urge to suppress thoughts of the assault spikes; he finds himself deliberately pushing the images and sensations away, forcing himself to think about his work instead. The threat monitoring that follows each memory compels David to constantly check behind him, even on the flat sidewalk. He scans every direction, looking for a shadow or a shadowed figure, and his pulse quickens at the slightest movement in his periphery. The anxiety is so strong that it sometimes delays his work: a brief pause to ensure the alley doors are locked, a check to confirm the security cameras are operational, a hesitation before entering a room that feels too confined. The longer a task takes, the more he suspects that something bad is unfolding. He feels a knot in his stomach, convinced that any delay could invite danger. The anticipation of threat intensifies his avoidance, which, in turn, leaves him less able to confront the memory in a controlled way. The avoidance behaviors reinforce his sense of threat. When he avoids the subway, he feels as if he is retreating from a real danger; when he delays tasks because he is constantly on guard, he confirms his belief that the world is hostile. Each time he engages in threat monitoring, the memory resurfaces, reminding him that he was once in a place that felt both small and vulnerable. He believes that by staying alert, he is protecting himself, but the protective effort only solidifies the belief that threats are imminent. David’s job as a social worker brings him into frequent contact with people who are in crisis, people who have experienced trauma, and people who speak about violence in their communities. In recent weeks he has felt the sting of his own trauma more acutely. During a session with a client who had been assaulted, David felt a surge of helplessness, and the memory of his own violation flooded back. He avoided the client’s apartment because the apartment’s narrow hallway reminded him of the alley. The avoidance caused friction with the client, who felt that David was not fully present. The fallout at work added a layer of shame that reinforced his sense that he had failed to keep his mind safe and his professional duties intact. After months of feeling trapped by the cycle, David finally reached a tipping point. The day after a client’s sudden anger escalated into a crisis because he had perceived David’s absence, David’s wife asked him what was wrong. He could no longer pretend that the memory of the assault was merely a past event. He had been avoiding closed spaces for weeks, checking behind him constantly, delaying routine tasks, and suppressing the thoughts that would bring him to his knees. The culmination of those behaviors had left him exhausted, fearful of both the world and his own mind. When his wife gently encouraged him to seek help, David realized that staying silent would only prolong the terror. He was afraid that confronting the memory might unravel his ability to protect himself, yet he was also hopeful that a therapist could help him untangle the loop of memory, threat, and avoidance that had become his everyday reality.
